--- title: "Scaling single-cell phenotyping with Cellpose and cloud GPU compute" date: 'January 1, 2025' abstract-title: "Summary" --- ## Abstract A reusable, cloud-scalable pipeline that pairs Cellpose-SAM segmentation with on-demand GPU compute (Modal + S3) for single-cell phenotyping of high-content microscopy, demonstrated on a two-species yeast panel (*Saccharomyces cerevisiae* vs. *Schizosaccharomyces pombe*). ---- :::{.callout-note title="AI usage disclosure" collapse="true"} This is a placeholder for the AI usage disclosure. Once all authors sign the AI code form on Airtable, SlackBot will message you an AI disclosure that you should place here. ::: ## Purpose High-content microscopy makes it easy to generate far more images than any single workstation can segment in a reasonable time. The bottleneck usually isn't the science — it's the plumbing: moving images, standing up GPUs, and getting consistent per-cell measurements out the other side. This pub shows one clean way to remove that bottleneck by combining a strong general-purpose segmentation model with elastic cloud GPU compute, so segmentation scales with your dataset instead of your hardware. **Key takeaways:** 1. Cellpose-SAM segmentation combined with cloud GPU compute is a reliable, flexible way to scale single-cell phenotyping across large microscopy datasets. 2. The phenotyping outputs resolve gross morphological differences between strains and conditions. **Who this is for:** Researchers and computational biologists doing high-throughput microscopy who want a segmentation and phenotyping pipeline, or who are weighing how to scale segmentation compute without building bespoke infrastructure. **What this is _not_:** No new biology, and not a Cellpose or Modal tutorial. **What you can do with it:** Run the accompanying notebook end-to-end on the example data, or lift the pattern (file I/O → segmentation → scale-out → per-cell measurements) into your own setup. ## How the pipeline fits together :::{.callout-note title="Draft figure" collapse="false"} A designed hero figure (in progress with Audrey) will replace the schematic below. The Mermaid diagram is a functional stand-in that captures the intended flow. ::: The workflow is a straight line from raw images to per-cell measurements, with one key property: the segmentation step is identical whether it runs on one machine or hundreds of GPU containers. Scale is a deployment choice, not a code rewrite. ```{mermaid} flowchart LR A["Brightfield ND2s
datasets/<id>/raw/"] --> B["File I/O + preprocessing
arcadia-microscopy-tools"] B --> C["Segmentation
Cellpose-SAM → label masks"] C --> D{"Scale-out
one worker per image"} D --> E["Derived artifacts
masks · overlays · measurements"] E --> F["Analysis
pooled per-cell morphology"] P["Plate map
well → strain"] --> F ``` 1. **Input:** brightfield ND2s in object storage, organized as `datasets//raw/`, with a plate map linking wells to strains. 2. **File I/O and preprocessing:** `arcadia-microscopy-tools` handles ND2 reading, channel and pixel-size metadata, and percentile rescaling. 3. **Segmentation:** Cellpose-SAM produces label masks; border-touching cells are dropped. 4. **Scale-out:** one worker per image is fanned across on-demand GPU containers, each reading from and writing to shared cloud storage. 5. **Outputs (`derived/`):** label-mask TIFFs, outline-overlay JPGs for QC, and per-cell measurement CSVs (regionprops, in microns where the pixel size is known). 6. **Analysis:** pooled per-cell measurements joined to the plate map for morphology comparisons across strains. ## Example dataset The demo runs on a two-species yeast panel: single-channel brightfield ND2s of two diploid strains with deliberately contrasting morphologies — the ovoid budding yeast *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* (BY4743) and the rod-shaped fission yeast *Schizosaccharomyces pombe* (SP286). The obvious shape difference makes this a clean illustration of differentiating cells by phenotype. | Species | Strain | Wells | Morphology | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | *S. cerevisiae* | `BY4743` | K01–K04, L01–L04 | ovoid budding yeast | | *S. pombe* | `SP286` | K05–K08, L05–L08 | rod-shaped fission yeast | The full well-to-strain mapping lives in `plate-map.csv` alongside this notebook. The multiple wells per species are technical replicates, not independent biological replicates — a caveat we return to in the analysis and limitations. **Acquisition (placeholder):** note the imaging modality, objective, and pixel size here, along with how wells map to ND2 filenames for this dataset. **Where to get the data:** the example images are archived publicly so any reader can pull them (Zenodo record link to be added). Internal readers with bucket access read the same images directly from S3. ## Demo: single-cell segmentation at scale The cells below run the full pipeline end to end: brightfield ND2s are segmented with Cellpose-SAM (via [`arcadia-microscopy-tools`](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/arcadia-microscopy-tools)) into label masks, QC overlays, and per-cell measurement tables. The same segmentation code runs in one of two interchangeable modes, chosen automatically so the notebook is runnable whether or not you have our cloud infrastructure. **Scaled mode (Modal + S3).** When the [Modal](https://modal.com/) client is authenticated and the `aws-s3-access-secret` (AWS credentials with read/write access to the `cloud-scaled-cell-phenotyping` bucket) is available, the heavy GPU compute is fanned out across Modal containers: each worker reads one ND2 from S3, segments it on a GPU, and writes the derived artifacts back to S3. The notebook only triggers the run and displays small previews returned by the workers. This is the path internal readers use, and it is what lets the pipeline keep pace with large datasets. **Local mode (no cloud account required).** When that infrastructure is not available, the notebook falls back to running the identical Cellpose-SAM pipeline on your own machine (CPU by default). It downloads a few example ND2s from the public [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/) archive over HTTPS, segments them locally, and writes the artifacts to a local folder. Because it runs on CPU, it is intentionally scoped to a few images via `limit`. Either way, `run_demo` returns the same result object, so every downstream cell is unchanged across modes — underscoring that scaling is transparent to the analysis. As each image finishes, a progress bar ticks forward and shows that file's cell count. Set the environment variable `CSCP_FORCE_LOCAL=1` to force the local path, or pass `backend="modal"` / `backend="local"` explicitly. ::: {#8264ef2a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} # import time # from analysis.runner import run_demo # # The example dataset: single-channel brightfield ND2s under `datasets//raw/`. DATASET_ID = "20260611_141152_330" # # The scaled Modal path segments the whole plate cheaply, so we process every well # # there; the local CPU fallback is capped to a few images to keep the demo fast. # # For the two-species comparison, make sure the local sample spans both cerevisiae # # (wells K01-K04/L01-L04) and pombe (K05-K08/L05-L08) wells; raise LIMIT if needed. # # LIMIT = None if modal_backend_available() else 3 # LIMIT = 3 # started = time.time() # run = run_demo(DATASET_ID, limit=LIMIT) # elapsed = time.time() - started # if run.backend == "modal": # print(f"[modal] Wrote artifacts to s3://cloud-scaled-cell-phenotyping/{run.output_prefix}/") # else: # print(f"[local] Wrote artifacts to {run.output_prefix}") # print(f"Segmented {len(run.results)} image(s), {len(run.failures)} failure(s) in {elapsed:.1f}s.") ``` ::: ## Visual QC: segmentation overlays The pipeline produces a small outline-overlay preview for each image (cell boundaries drawn on the brightfield image). We display a few here as a quick visual QC of the segmentation. Good segmentation traces each cell's boundary tightly without merging neighbors or splitting single cells; the pipeline drops cells touching the image border, since their measurements would be biased by truncation. ::: {#b0587d06 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # from pathlib import Path # from IPython.display import Image as IPyImage # from IPython.display import display # for summary in run.results[:1]: # overlay_path = summary.get("local_overlay") # if overlay_path: # print(f"{Path(summary['input']).name}: {summary['n_cells']} cells") # display(IPyImage(filename=overlay_path, width=500)) ``` ::: ## Per-cell phenotyping outputs The pipeline also produces per-cell measurements (regionprops, converted to microns where the pixel size is known): one row per cell, with shape features such as area, eccentricity, and axis lengths. We pool them across the segmented images and join each cell to its species via the plate map (well → species), so every cell carries a species label for the analysis that follows. The segmentation workers also write these tables to `derived//measurements/` in shared storage, so you don't have to re-segment to analyze them. By default we use the measurements from the run above, but setting `MEASUREMENTS_SOURCE` in the next cell to `"auto"` loads the full precomputed table for **every** well — from the S3 bucket (internal readers) or the public Zenodo archive (external readers). That's the easiest way to get both species in the analysis when the local demo only segmented a few images. ::: {#d0ee1968 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import re from pathlib import Path import pandas as pd from analysis.measurements import load_measurements # Where the per-cell measurements come from: # "run" - the table produced by the demo run above (only the images it # segmented; in local mode that is just LIMIT images from one species). # "auto" - load the full precomputed table for the whole plate without # re-segmenting, from S3 (internal) or Zenodo (external). Use this to # analyze every well and both species. # "modal" / "zenodo" - force the S3 or Zenodo source explicitly. MEASUREMENTS_SOURCE = "auto" ``` ::: ::: {#dd328ce2 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Code to load per-cell measurements"} if MEASUREMENTS_SOURCE == "run": measurements = run.measurements.copy() else: measurements = load_measurements(DATASET_ID, source=MEASUREMENTS_SOURCE) def _find_plate_map() -> Path: for candidate in (Path("plate-map.csv"), Path("../plate-map.csv")): if candidate.exists(): return candidate raise FileNotFoundError("plate-map.csv not found next to the notebook or its parent.") plate_map = pd.read_csv(_find_plate_map()) def well_from_name(name: str) -> str | None: """Pull a plate-well token (e.g. 'K01', 'WellL8') from an image name. DRAFT NOTE: confirm this matches the ND2 naming convention for your dataset. It normalizes to the plate-map form (uppercase row letter + zero-padded column). Rows span A-P so 384-well layouts (this dataset uses rows K/L) are covered. """ match = re.search(r"(?:well[ _-]?)?([A-P])0*([1-9][0-9]?)", name, flags=re.IGNORECASE) if not match: return None return f"{match.group(1).upper()}{int(match.group(2)):02d}" measurements["well"] = measurements["image"].map(well_from_name) labeled = measurements.merge(plate_map[["well", "species", "strain"]], on="well", how="left") n_unmapped = int(labeled["species"].isna().sum()) if n_unmapped: print( f"Warning: {n_unmapped} cell(s) had no species match; check well_from_name vs. your filenames." ) print(f"{len(labeled)} cells across {labeled['species'].nunique()} species.") labeled.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 113379 cells across 2 species. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Shape alone separates the two species The per-cell measurements are the pipeline's actual product, so the fair test of the pipeline is whether they support the kind of analysis you'd want to do next. We ask the simplest version of that question: given nothing but per-cell shape, can you tell the two yeasts apart? *S. cerevisiae* is an ovoid budding yeast and *S. pombe* is a rod, so the expected answer is yes — and that's the point. A pipeline that failed this test wouldn't be worth scaling. We're testing the measurements, not discovering biology. Three steps follow. First we look at the joint distribution of the two features that should carry most of the signal, cell area and eccentricity. Then we rank every shape feature by how well it separates the species on its own. Finally we train a random forest on all nine shape features and hold out an entire well at a time, which is the strictest test this dataset can support. Before any of that, we gate on cell area. Segmentation returns some objects that aren't single cells: fragments and debris at the small end, and clumps that Cellpose resolved as a single mask at the large end (the largest object in the full-plate table is about 1,270 µm², roughly fifty times the median *S. cerevisiae* cell). We keep objects between 5 and 100 µm², an area-equivalent circular diameter of 2.5–11.3 µm, which brackets a plausible single yeast cell. The gate is deliberately loose: it drops about 1% of objects and isn't tuned to flatter the analysis. ::: {#7a56e334 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Code to set up the analysis and gate on cell area"} import arcadia_pycolor as apc import numpy as np import plotly.graph_objects as go from plotly.subplots import make_subplots apc.plotly.setup() GROUP_COL = "species" REFERENCE = "cerevisiae" # the species the others are compared against POSITIVE = "pombe" # the "positive" class for AUC, ROC, and the confusion matrix AREA_COL = "area_um2" if "area_um2" in labeled.columns else "area" AREA_LABEL = "cell area (µm²)" if AREA_COL == "area_um2" else "cell area (px)" # Plausible-single-cell gate. 5-100 µm² is an area-equivalent circular diameter of # 2.5-11.3 µm: below it, debris and partial masks; above it, merged clumps. MIN_AREA_UM2 = 5.0 MAX_AREA_UM2 = 100.0 measured = labeled.dropna(subset=[GROUP_COL, AREA_COL]) # The gate is written in µm², so it only applies when the pixel size was known. in_gate = ( measured[AREA_COL].between(MIN_AREA_UM2, MAX_AREA_UM2) if AREA_COL == "area_um2" else pd.Series(True, index=measured.index) ) analysis_df = measured.loc[in_gate].copy() present = list(analysis_df[GROUP_COL].unique()) groups = ([REFERENCE] if REFERENCE in present else []) + sorted( g for g in present if g != REFERENCE ) # Italicized "S. pombe"-style labels and a stable color per species, from the plate map. genus_by_species = plate_map.drop_duplicates(GROUP_COL).set_index(GROUP_COL)["genus"] DISPLAY = {species: f"{genus_by_species[species][0]}. {species}" for species in groups} COLORS = dict( zip(groups, [apc.aegean.hex_code, apc.amber.hex_code, apc.seaweed.hex_code], strict=False) ) n_dropped = int((~in_gate).sum()) print( f"{len(analysis_df):,} of {len(measured):,} cells pass the " f"{MIN_AREA_UM2:g}-{MAX_AREA_UM2:g} µm² gate " f"({n_dropped:,} dropped, {n_dropped / len(measured):.2%})." ) print( f"{len(groups)} species across {analysis_df['well'].nunique()} well(s) and " f"{analysis_df['image'].nunique()} image(s): {', '.join(groups)}" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 112,157 of 113,379 cells pass the 5-100 µm² gate (1,222 dropped, 1.08%). 2 species across 16 well(s) and 64 image(s): cerevisiae, pombe ``` ::: ::: ::: {#fcc4b8f6 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Code for the area-vs-eccentricity figure"} # Every cell is used for the marginal boxes; the scatter shows a random subsample per # species, since 112,000 overplotted markers read as two solid blobs (and bloat the page). POINTS_PER_SPECIES = 5000 rng = np.random.default_rng(0) def box_stats(values): """Quartiles and Tukey fences for a Plotly box trace built from precomputed statistics.""" q1, median, q3 = np.percentile(values, [25, 50, 75]) iqr = q3 - q1 return dict( q1=[q1], median=[median], q3=[q3], lowerfence=[max(values.min(), q1 - 1.5 * iqr)], upperfence=[min(values.max(), q3 + 1.5 * iqr)], mean=[values.mean()], ) fig = make_subplots( rows=2, cols=2, column_widths=[0.85, 0.15], row_heights=[0.15, 0.85], shared_xaxes=True, shared_yaxes=True, horizontal_spacing=0.02, vertical_spacing=0.02, ) for species in groups: cells = analysis_df[analysis_df[GROUP_COL] == species] color = COLORS[species] shown = cells.iloc[ rng.choice(len(cells), size=min(POINTS_PER_SPECIES, len(cells)), replace=False) ] fig.add_trace( go.Scattergl( x=shown[AREA_COL], y=shown["eccentricity"], mode="markers", showlegend=False, marker=dict(color=color, size=3, opacity=0.4, line=dict(width=0)), hovertemplate=f"{species}
area %{{x:.1f}} µm²
ecc. %{{y:.2f}}", ), row=2, col=1, ) # A legend-only proxy, so the key shows a full-size, full-opacity marker. fig.add_trace( go.Scatter( x=[None], y=[None], mode="markers", name=f"{DISPLAY[species]} (n = {len(cells):,})", marker=dict(color=color, size=9), ), row=2, col=1, ) box_kwargs = dict( showlegend=False, fillcolor=color, line=dict(color=apc.charcoal.hex_code, width=1), width=0.45, hoverinfo="skip", ) fig.add_trace( go.Box(**box_stats(cells[AREA_COL].to_numpy()), y=[species], orientation="h", **box_kwargs), row=1, col=1, ) fig.add_trace( go.Box(**box_stats(cells["eccentricity"].to_numpy()), x=[species], **box_kwargs), row=2, col=2, ) fig.update_xaxes(title_text=AREA_LABEL, range=[0, MAX_AREA_UM2], row=2, col=1) fig.update_yaxes(title_text="eccentricity", range=[0, 1.02], row=2, col=1) for row, col in ((1, 1), (2, 2)): # the marginals borrow their scale from the scatter fig.update_xaxes(showticklabels=False, ticks="", showline=False, row=row, col=col) fig.update_yaxes(showticklabels=False, ticks="", showline=False, row=row, col=col) fig.update_layout( width=720, height=560, title="Area and eccentricity split the panel into two populations", legend=dict( x=0.99, y=0.03, xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom", bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.75)" ), ) apc.plotly.style_plot(fig, monospaced_axes="xy", row=2, col=1) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The two clouds barely touch. *S. pombe* traces a tight arc, which is what fission yeast morphology predicts: it grows by extending its tips at roughly constant width, so a cell gets larger and more elongated at the same time, and area and eccentricity rise together over the cell cycle. *S. cerevisiae* instead fills a broad, rounder cloud with a tail toward small area and low eccentricity — mostly small buds. The marginal boxes show where the separation actually comes from: the area distributions overlap substantially, since a large budding yeast is the size of a small fission yeast, while the eccentricity distributions hardly overlap at all. ### Ranking every shape feature Area and eccentricity are two of the nine shape features the pipeline reports. To rank all of them, we use the area under the ROC curve for each feature on its own — the probability that a randomly chosen *S. pombe* cell scores higher than a randomly chosen *S. cerevisiae* cell. An AUC of 0.5 means the feature is useless and 1.0 means the two distributions don't overlap at all. It's a rank statistic, so the long tails in these distributions don't distort it. We report a p-value as well, but not the one you might expect. A Mann–Whitney test across all 112,000 cells returns p ≈ 0 for every feature, which tells you nothing: cells from the same well share a field of view, a focus plane, and an illumination profile, so a cell-level test is counting pseudoreplicates. The p-value below compares the sixteen well-level medians instead, eight per species. That's the unit of replication this plate actually supports, and with eight versus eight the smallest attainable two-sided p-value is 1.6 × 10⁻⁴. Several features sit exactly on that floor, meaning the well medians separate perfectly. They're technical replicates, so the test speaks to consistency across wells, not to the species. ::: {#c472595a .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Code to rank shape features by how well each one separates the species"} from scipy.stats import mannwhitneyu from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score # Shape only. Orientation is an arbitrary lab-frame angle, the centroids are positions, and # the brightfield intensities describe illumination as much as they describe the cell. FEATURES = { "area_um2": "area (µm²)", "area_convex_um2": "convex area (µm²)", "perimeter_um": "perimeter (µm)", "axis_major_length_um": "major axis (µm)", "axis_minor_length_um": "minor axis (µm)", "eccentricity": "eccentricity", "solidity": "solidity", "circularity": "circularity", "volume_um3": "volume (µm³)", } FEATURES = {col: label for col, label in FEATURES.items() if col in analysis_df.columns} is_positive = (analysis_df[GROUP_COL] == POSITIVE).to_numpy() well_medians = analysis_df.groupby(["well", GROUP_COL])[list(FEATURES)].median().reset_index() rows = [] for col, label in FEATURES.items(): auc = roc_auc_score(is_positive, analysis_df[col]) _, p_well = mannwhitneyu( well_medians.loc[well_medians[GROUP_COL] == POSITIVE, col], well_medians.loc[well_medians[GROUP_COL] == REFERENCE, col], alternative="two-sided", ) rows.append( { "feature": label, f"median, {REFERENCE}": round(analysis_df.loc[~is_positive, col].median(), 2), f"median, {POSITIVE}": round(analysis_df.loc[is_positive, col].median(), 2), # Flip AUCs below 0.5 so every feature is scored in its discriminating direction. "AUC": round(max(auc, 1 - auc), 3), "well-level p": f"{p_well:.1e}", } ) feature_stats = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("AUC", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True) feature_stats ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Eccentricity leads at an AUC of 0.995, with circularity and major-axis length close behind — all three are measuring elongation. The size features land lower (area at 0.951), and the two features that describe neither elongation nor size, solidity and minor-axis length, are barely better than a coin flip. That last result is the one worth noting: fission yeast and budding yeast are about the same width, so a classifier that only knew cell width would have almost nothing to work with. ### A classifier that has never seen the well it's scoring Ranking features one at a time ignores the possibility that combinations do better, and a random forest on all nine features answers that — but only if it's evaluated carefully. Splitting cells at random into train and test sets would be close to meaningless here, for the same reason the cell-level p-value was: two cells from the same image share so much context that a model can partly memorize the well instead of learning the shape. So we hold out whole wells. Sixteen times over, we train on fifteen wells and predict every cell in the sixteenth, so every prediction below comes from a model that never saw that well. We also subsample to 2,000 cells per well, which balances the two species (the plate has roughly 3.5× more *S. cerevisiae* cells than *S. pombe*) and keeps the whole cross-validation to a few tens of seconds on a laptop. One consequence of holding out wells is worth stating plainly: each held-out well contains a single species, so a per-fold ROC curve is undefined. Per-fold accuracy is still well defined — it's the fraction of that well's cells assigned to the right species — and the ROC curve is computed once, on the pooled out-of-fold predictions. ::: {#f3c72281 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, balanced_accuracy_score, confusion_matrix, roc_curve from sklearn.model_selection import LeaveOneGroupOut CELLS_PER_WELL = 2000 RANDOM_STATE = 0 # Shuffle once, then take the first N rows of each well: a per-well subsample that also # balances the species, since the plate has the same number of wells for each. balanced = ( analysis_df.sample(frac=1.0, random_state=RANDOM_STATE) .groupby("well") .head(CELLS_PER_WELL) .reset_index(drop=True) ) X = balanced[list(FEATURES)].to_numpy() y = (balanced[GROUP_COL] == POSITIVE).to_numpy().astype(int) wells = balanced["well"].to_numpy() fold_species = balanced[GROUP_COL].to_numpy() oof_proba = np.zeros(len(y)) fold_rows = [] for train_idx, test_idx in LeaveOneGroupOut().split(X, y, groups=wells): forest = RandomForestClassifier( n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=5, n_jobs=-1, random_state=RANDOM_STATE ) forest.fit(X[train_idx], y[train_idx]) oof_proba[test_idx] = forest.predict_proba(X[test_idx])[:, 1] fold_rows.append( { "well": wells[test_idx][0], "species": fold_species[test_idx][0], "n_cells": len(test_idx), "accuracy": accuracy_score(y[test_idx], (oof_proba[test_idx] >= 0.5).astype(int)), } ) oof_pred = (oof_proba >= 0.5).astype(int) accuracy = accuracy_score(y, oof_pred) balanced_acc = balanced_accuracy_score(y, oof_pred) auc = roc_auc_score(y, oof_proba) folds = pd.DataFrame(fold_rows).sort_values(["species", "well"]) print(f"{len(balanced):,} cells | {len(FEATURES)} features | {len(folds)} leave-one-well-out folds") print( f"accuracy {accuracy:.3f} | balanced accuracy {balanced_acc:.3f} | AUC {auc:.4f} | " f"per-well accuracy {folds['accuracy'].min():.3f}-{folds['accuracy'].max():.3f}" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 32,000 cells | 9 features | 16 leave-one-well-out folds accuracy 0.986 | balanced accuracy 0.986 | AUC 0.9963 | per-well accuracy 0.973-0.997 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#485d5dde .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Code for the classifier figure"} # The best single feature, for comparison against the full model on the same ROC axes. BEST_SINGLE = feature_stats.loc[0, "feature"] best_col = next(col for col, label in FEATURES.items() if label == BEST_SINGLE) single_values = balanced[best_col].to_numpy() single_auc = roc_auc_score(y, single_values) if single_auc < 0.5: # score the feature in whichever direction discriminates single_values, single_auc = -single_values, 1 - single_auc fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y, oof_proba) single_fpr, single_tpr, _ = roc_curve(y, single_values) matrix = confusion_matrix(y, oof_pred) matrix_rate = matrix / matrix.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True) class_order = [REFERENCE, POSITIVE] class_labels = [DISPLAY[species] for species in class_order] fig2 = make_subplots( rows=1, cols=3, column_widths=[0.31, 0.36, 0.33], horizontal_spacing=0.11, subplot_titles=( "Out-of-fold confusion matrix", "Out-of-fold ROC", "Accuracy per held-out well", ), ) fig2.add_trace( go.Heatmap( z=matrix_rate, x=class_labels, y=class_labels, text=[ [f"{matrix[i, j]:,}
{matrix_rate[i, j]:.1%}" for j in range(len(class_order))] for i in range(len(class_order)) ], texttemplate="%{text}", textfont=dict(size=12), colorscale=[[0.0, apc.zephyr.hex_code], [1.0, apc.aegean.hex_code]], zmin=0, zmax=1, showscale=False, hoverinfo="skip", ), row=1, col=1, ) fig2.update_xaxes(title_text="predicted", row=1, col=1) fig2.update_yaxes(title_text="true", autorange="reversed", row=1, col=1) fig2.add_trace( go.Scatter( x=[0, 1], y=[0, 1], mode="lines", line=dict(color=apc.chateau.hex_code, width=1, dash="dot"), showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip", ), row=1, col=2, ) fig2.add_trace( go.Scatter( x=fpr, y=tpr, mode="lines", line=dict(color=apc.aster.hex_code, width=4), showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip", ), row=1, col=2, ) # Drawn on top of the full model, because the overlap is the point. fig2.add_trace( go.Scatter( x=single_fpr, y=single_tpr, mode="lines", line=dict(color=apc.bark.hex_code, width=1.5, dash="dash"), showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip", ), row=1, col=2, ) fig2.add_annotation( x=0.35, y=0.30, xref="x2", yref="y2", xanchor="left", align="left", showarrow=False, text=f"all {len(FEATURES)} features
AUC {auc:.3f}", font=dict(color=apc.aster.hex_code, size=12), ) fig2.add_annotation( x=0.35, y=0.08, xref="x2", yref="y2", xanchor="left", align="left", showarrow=False, text=f"{BEST_SINGLE} alone
AUC {single_auc:.3f}", font=dict(color=apc.bark.hex_code, size=12), ) fig2.update_xaxes(title_text="false positive rate", range=[-0.02, 1.02], row=1, col=2) fig2.update_yaxes(title_text="true positive rate", range=[-0.02, 1.02], row=1, col=2) for species in class_order: per_well = folds[folds["species"] == species] fig2.add_trace( go.Scatter( x=per_well["accuracy"], y=per_well["well"], mode="markers", showlegend=False, marker=dict(color=COLORS[species], size=9, line=dict(width=0)), hovertemplate="%{y}: %{x:.3f}", ), row=1, col=3, ) fig2.add_vline( x=accuracy, line=dict(color=apc.charcoal.hex_code, width=1, dash="dot"), row=1, col=3 ) fig2.update_xaxes(title_text="accuracy", range=[0.95, 1.005], tickformat=".2f", row=1, col=3) fig2.update_yaxes(type="category", dtick=1, autorange="reversed", row=1, col=3) fig2.update_layout( width=1000, height=480, margin=dict(t=90), title=dict(text="Shape alone identifies the species in wells the model never saw", y=0.97), ) for col in (1, 2, 3): apc.plotly.style_plot(fig2, row=1, col=col) fig2.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Shape alone identifies the species for 98.6% of cells in wells the model never saw, and the per-well accuracies sit in a tight band from 97.3% to 99.7% with no well behaving strangely. That consistency is the useful result. It says the pipeline's measurements are stable across wells and images, which is what you need before pointing it at a plate where you don't already know the answer. It's also worth noticing how little the classifier adds. Eccentricity on its own reaches an AUC of 0.995 against the full model's 0.996, so this is a nearly one-dimensional problem dressed up as a nine-dimensional one — which is exactly what you'd expect from two species chosen for contrasting shapes. That's a property of the example, not of the method. On a panel where the phenotype is subtler, the multivariate model is where the signal would come from, and the leave-one-well-out design is what would keep the estimate honest. We draw no biological conclusions. The wells within a species are technical replicates from a single experiment: enough to show that the pipeline produces stable, species-resolved phenotypes, and not enough to say anything about the organisms. ## Limitations - **Scope of the demo:** gross morphology only, from single-channel brightfield images. Staining- or fluorescence-based phenotyping is a natural extension, not shown here. - **Compute and cost:** the scaled path relies on paid GPU compute and cloud storage. The local CPU fallback is deliberately scoped to a few images so anyone can reproduce the core result without an account, but it does not exercise the scale-out. - **Replication:** a single dataset with multiple wells per species (technical, not biological, replicates) — enough to show the pipeline works, not to make claims about the organisms. ## Future directions - Fluorescence and intensity phenotyping (e.g., BODIPY-stained yeast, or *Chlorella* chlorophyll autofluorescence). - Larger panels and full-plate throughput, and additional organisms. ## Acknowledgements, references, and appendix **Acknowledgements:** overview-figure design by Audrey; contributors and author list to be added. **Tools and references:** [`arcadia-microscopy-tools`](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/arcadia-microscopy-tools) (file I/O, preprocessing, measurements), Cellpose-SAM (segmentation), [Modal](https://modal.com/) (on-demand GPU compute), and Amazon S3 (shared storage). Full citations to be added. **Run it yourself:** environment setup and step-by-step run instructions for both modes live in the repository README and project docs, kept out of the narrative so this pub reads as a blog post rather than a manual. **Appendix (optional):** the segmentation knobs exposed by `SegmentConfig` — `diameter`, `flow_threshold`, `cellprob_threshold`, and the `percentile_low`/`percentile_high` contrast window — plus scaling parameters (`gpu`, `max_containers`) forwarded to the Modal workers.
